content.summary_of_the_paper:
A new method for neural program synthesis via composition is presented. More precisely, the method operates by first predicting a sequence of "task embeddings", which are then individually expanded into a short programs, with the final result being the concatenation of the generated short programs.
The paper also introduces a new synthetic dataset on a string manipulation DSL, which is then used to compare different ablations of the model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* (+) The idea of decomposing longer target programs is interresting and promising.
* (-) The paper writing is not sufficiently clear to fully understand the proposed method.
* (-) The experiments are weak: using a new dataset likely to be unrepresentative of realistic programs (cf. the similarly constructed DeepCoder dataset and its subsequent criticism) only ablations of the presented model are evaluated.
* (-) The relationship to existing work is not discussed well. https://openreview.net/forum?id=HL5l13dbybq may be a good starting point to find relevant references (in particular, BUSTLE seems highly relevant, even though it performs its search top-down).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is largely well-written and easy to follow, but core technical details in Sect. 4 remain unclear (see below). Similarly, experimental details are missing.

The experiments are performed on a new synthetic dataset, using only models written and trained by the authors. That makes it hard to understand how the proposed method compares to existing methods.

I believe the idea of doing top-down decomposition using the proposed task embeddings is novel. However, the idea is complementary to the BUSTLE algorithm (Odena et al, ICLR'20), which performs bottom-up synthesis using so-called property signatures. In many ways, the method proposed here is its complement, and similar to a neural version of the idea in Sect. 5 of https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.09030.pdf. This does not take away from the novelty of actually executing this, but it would be helpful if the authors would compare more with the existing literature.

Notes:
* Fig. 1: "Boundary :=" -> "Boundary b :="
* Sect. 4.2: How do you select meaningful compositions? How is composition defined in this domain anyway? I couldn't quite understand the examples in Fig. 4: is the input implicit? Are all examples concatenations?
* Sect. 4.3: "A task interpreter $e_\eta$ learns to interpret given task specifications (i.e. string I/O pairs)" - what does "interpret" mean here?
* Sect. 4.3: "We task specifications from [...]" - this sentence is not grammatical, and I do not understand what it means.
* Sect. 4.3: " produces task embeddings until a long program that satisfies the task specification is generated" - what does "satisfies" mean here? How is this determined?
content.summary_of_the_review:
I recommend to reject the submission at this time for two reasons:
(1) The writing needs to be substantially improved to make sure that the authors' ideas are precisely communicated and others can understand and reproduce their work. This could conceivably be fixed in a simple iteration on the current paper.
(2) The experiments need to be much stronger to show the value of the idea. In particular, evaluation needs to happen on a dataset on which other papers have been evaluated on, as this is not a novel task. Any dataset with "longer" programs (of more >3 lines) would do, but maybe something like MTPB from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.13474.pdf would be most appropriate. I do not think that this can happen in the ICLR review process.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new framework to synthesize Domain-Specific Language (DSL) programs of longer length, which leverages a multi-stage hierarchical  composition process to first train a model to generate smaller program gadgets that handle specific parts of overall objective program features (e.g., one transformation rule of input-output string pairs), and then a second model for combining previously learned program gadgets to form up complete programs. Ablational evaluation results in the paper show that compared to model variants of different designs, the proposed model achieves the highest execution correctness over tested DSL programs, especially in cases of long programs.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
+ Intuitively, the idea of learning to first synthesize program gadgets, and then combine them hierarchically makes sense.
+ Being able to synthesize long programs are of urgent importance for neural program synthesizer, and thus a challenge to be addressed.

Weaknesses
- I cannot seem to find any experimental comparison between HNPS and prior state-of-the-arts. Despite the statement "...than the programs considered in prior program synthesis works." in the paper abstract, as well as a list of closely related works in Section 2, there seem to be no head-to-head comparison in Section 5.3 with prior research -- only numbers present in this section are from "artificial baselines" which are basically ablational versions of the HNPS framework itself. I am not convinced by this evaluation setup. If authors believe none of state-of-the-arts is directly comparable (which does not seem to be the case given their wording in Section 2), they should offer explanations and justifications. Without these evidences, it is very hard for me to judge on how this work stands with prior literature/efforts.
- The proposed framework seems to be tightly bounded to specific types of DSL programing tasks. Specifically, learning program gadgets (that transform strings) and then sequentially ordering them to form up complete programs maps to a limited scope of programs -- e.g., what if there are interrelationships/dependencies among different gadgets? What if there are synthesis goals that cannot be achieved by simply piling up small program gadgets (that are all in similar formats, and for similar local objectives)? I am unsure if this DSL program synthesis task is the most widely used one in the domain of program synthesis, but would like to at least see more discussions on how the synthesis programs in this field is evaluated upon. If not, I suggest authors provide more experimental results on other types of program synthesis tasks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think this paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. I especially appreciated the appendix of the paper, which very clearly describes model details etc. that were omitted from the main body.

I think the idea of hierarchically composing programs is natural but of novelty. There is not much of model improvement inside the proposed framework though.

I cannot find any code release from the manuscript. With detailed model hyper-parameters, I think it is possible to reproduce results from the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, the idea of this paper is interesting and of some novelty, especially for addressing the length issue in particular program synthesis problems (e.g., DSL programs for transforming strings), while I do not know if it can be applied to more general-purpose program synthesis tasks. The evaluations conducted in this paper are too limited and thus make it hard to assess the real improvement of the proposed approach compared to prior state-of-the-arts.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The objective of this paper is to synthesize longer or more complex programs. Towards this, the authors propose a hierarchical model which recursively decodes the embedding of I/O examples into intermediate embeddings and uses a program generator to synthesize short programs from the intermediate embeddings. The resulting model HNPS is evaluated on programs in a string transformation domain.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The proposal in the paper is interesting. The authors prepare two separate datasets: short and composed. The programs and their I/O examples are generated synthetically. An embedding model from I/O examples and a program decoder are trained on the short dataset. The embedding model is then trained on the composed dataset jointly with a program composer and the decoder, by providing supervision at the intermediate stages.

The experimental evaluation is not convincing for multiple reasons:
1) The objective is to scale to longer and more complex programs, but the long dataset used for evaluation only contains 2-4 expressions. This dataset cannot be said to be substantially longer or more complex. Thus, the evaluation falls short of the promised scalability.
2) The measure of success is execution accuracy which counts the percentage of I/O examples satisfied. This degrades quickly with more tokens per programs. Note that the long programs can be at most 4 expressions and the programs generated by HNPS achieve only 2% execution accuracy. What is the percentage of programs that pass all I/O examples across the lengths? In what sense can we say that synthesis has succeeded if I/O examples are failing?
3) The results are presented on a simple DSL. General purpose programs are more complex and much longer. They have variables, side-effects and control statements. The paper does not provide any evidence about improving scalability for this.
4) There are many published works that deal with string transformations and DSL based synthesis. There is no comparison to any published baseline so it is not possible to put this improvements in context.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I request the authors to clarify the following:
1) Are the dataset sizes in Sec 5.1 after programs with fewer than 20 examples are discarded or before? If the latter, what the actual dataset sizes?
2) The discussion on embedding space in Sec 5.3.2 is confusing to me. The last sentence on page 8 states that distance after changing critical tokens is smaller compared to distance after changing non-critical tokens. The first sentence on page 9 states that the embedding after changing critical tokens are placed further?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes hierarchical program synthesis and evaluates it on string transformation programs in a DSL. The scale and complexity of programs, the correctness of synthesized programs, lack of strong baselines and restrictive nature of the domain/DSL limit the applicability of the program synthesizer.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a hierarchical neural method for solving program synthesis tasks. First, the system learns an embedding space for short programs. Then, the system trains another model that learns to produce vectors in the latent space produced in the first step. These latent vectors are decoded and the resulting programs combined in the a larger program. Instead of synthesizing programs token by token, the system synthesizes programs short-program by short-program. 

Empirical evaluation on string manipulation tasks shows that the hierarchical neural method outperforms baseline systems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

I believe the authors are on the right track for learning models for solving program synthesis tasks. This paper follows a similar line of research from the LEAPS work, which is another paper recently published on this topic. In this line of research one transfers the daunting task of searching for a program in program spaces to a smoother latent space. I really like this research direction. However, this paper still misses some important points (see below) and it might early for its publication. 

This paper not only uses the idea of searching in latent spaces, but also the idea of synthesizing small programs as opposed to one token at a time. I also think this is a great idea and a merit of this paper. 

Weaknesses

Although I really like the idea of the paper, I think it misses important baselines and the empirical design isn't the correct one. 

Let's start with baselines. Program synthesis is a very broad field, touching Programming Language, Computer Games, AI, and ML communities. This paper seems to only cite papers from the ML community. I would like to invite the authors to at least recognize that other communities are also doing interesting work on program synthesis. This leads me back to the baselines. What about search algorithms that are guided by a cost function (some cost functions are a neural network)? Aren't those considered neural program synthesis? Two baselines come to mind: Probe [1] and Bustle [2]. I am not saying your system has to outperform Probe and Bustle to be published. But we should at least know how they compare and the current paper should discuss strengths and weaknesses of these approaches. 

Both Probe and Bustle perform bottom-up search, which works by combining smaller programs into larger programs. This is exactly the idea behind the current paper. I am very curious to see a comparison of these methods. I would even go further and add a much simpler baseline that only performs bottom-up search with no neural guidance---vanilla bottom-up search. 

The accuracy metric might also be misleading. While a program can be very accurate, it can still fail to solve a problem. I would be curious to see the accuracy of the vanilla bottom-up search in the test problems. Why use accuracy instead of number of problems solved? 

Another weakness is related to the test set used to evaluate the models. The test problems are coming from the same distribution of programs and strings used to train the model. This would be fine if in real life we also encountered similar problems, but it is unlikely we face problems formulated with randomly generated strings and solved with randomly generated programs. There is a standard benchmark set of string manipulation tasks that was used several times in the Sygus competition: https://sygus.org/. The sygus set is formed of real-world problems. 

References

[1] Barke, S., Peleg, H., & Polikarpova, N. (2020). Just-in-time learning for bottom-up enumerative synthesis. Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages, 4 (OOPSLA), 1–29

[2] Odena, A., Shi, K., Bieber, D., Singh, R., Sutton, C., & Dai, H. (2021). BUSTLE: bottom-up program synthesis through learning-guided exploration. In 9th International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2021, Virtual Event, Austria, May 3-7, 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

The paper is well written for who wants to have a general idea of how the method works. The paper lacks important information, however. 

1. What is the procedure for generating random strings? 
2. How are the random programs generated? Is there any mechanism to avoid bloating (this term comes from the genetic programming literature)?
3. How are the programs combined? Are they placed one next to the other or a program is provided as input to another program? If the latter, then how to decide which parameter slot to use? 
4. What is a one-expression long program? 

Quality

While the ablation studies are excellent, I miss a few baseline algorithms. The empirical set up is also not ideal as the test set is formed by random programs and random strings, so it is hard to conclude that the results will generalize to real-world problems. 

Novelty

The idea of performing synthesis by combining smaller programs isn't exactly novel as this is exactly what bottom-up search does. Using this idea in the context of neural program generation is novel and I really like it! 

Reproducibility

As I mentioned above, the paper lacks important information. My current guess is that I would be unable to reproduce the results of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper presents interesting ideas, but it seems a bit early for publication. The empirical setting isn't ideal as the experiments miss baselines and the test set isn't a realistic one.

content.title: Hierarchical Neural Program Synthesis
content.abstract: Program synthesis aims to automatically construct human-readable programs that satisfy given task specifications such as input/output pairs or demonstrations. Recent works have demonstrated encouraging results in a variety of domains such as string transformation, tensor manipulation, and describing behaviors of embodied agents. Most existing program synthesis methods are designed to synthesize programs from scratch, generating a program token by token, line by line. This fundamentally prevents these methods from scaling up to synthesize programs that are longer or more complex. In this work, we present a scalable program synthesis framework that instead synthesizes a program by hierarchically composing programs. Specifically, we first learn a task embedding space and a program decoder that can decode a task embedding into a program. Then, we train a high-level module to comprehend the task specification (e.g. input/output pairs or demonstrations) from long programs and produce a sequence of task embeddings, which are then decoded by the program decoder and composed to yield the synthesized program. We extensively evaluate our proposed framework in a string transformation domain with input/output pairs. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework can synthesize programs that are significantly longer and more complex than the programs considered in prior program synthesis works
